body:
The playbook you read is not wrong. It covers only the visible part of each fortune. Strip each legend down and you find an asset the books cannot hand you. For Buffett it was cheap, uncallable capital and seventy years of time. For Lynch it was access and a workload that burned him out at 46. For Damani it was a company he built. For Jhunjhunwala it was an era, borrowed money, a bear market on the right side and one stock that went up a thousandfold. For Porinju it was a tolerance for losing two-thirds. For Sundar it was an audience. For Jane Street it was speed and balance sheet. Knowledge was the entry ticket, and it has been widely shared for decades. Because everyone now has it, it decides less than ever, which is exactly what the paradox of skill predicts.

The useful reframing is to stop asking "how do I find the next Titan" and start asking which structural advantage you have that a fund or an algorithm does not. For most Indian professionals the honest answer is three things: specialised knowledge of one industry, the freedom to own small companies and hold them for a decade without anyone redeeming you, and the ability to save hard and stay out of the games built to transfer money from individuals to institutions. Built over 25–30 years, those produce real wealth. Extreme wealth still comes mostly from founding something, and from the luck that no amount of reading can manufacture.

Motilal Oswal's 2020–25 study named BSE the fastest wealth creator. Drawdowns: −73% (2017–20, before), −55% (Mar 2022–Mar 2023), −35% (Jan–Mar 2025). Revenue FY23 ₹925 cr → FY26 ₹5,124 cr; OPM 34% → 68%; ROCE 12% → 60%. Early signal: in May 2023 BSE relaunched Sensex/Bankex derivatives (contract-design details unverified). Exchange-published daily options premium share was the alt-data: 11.4% (Oct 2024) → 24.4% (Sep 2025) → 26.8% (Q3 FY26). The SEBI Nov 2024 rule allowing one weekly index expiry per exchange made BSE's Sensex expiry a scarce slot. A near-zero marginal cost platform meant each volume gain flowed to profit. In Mar 2023 the stock was at P/E ~29 with EPS about to grow 12x. Risks: regulatory single point of failure (expiry-day changes, talk of monthly-only expiries, STT); its customers are mostly losing retail F&O traders (see insight:sebi-fo-losses). Lesson: exchange operating leverage plus a free, daily market-share series let an alert investor size the earnings inflection early.

1. **For an MNC subsidiary, the AGM-notice RPT annex is the richest document in the set.** SEBI's Jun-2025 "minimum information" standard forces pricing formulas (cost +11%, +14%, +5%), the royalty rate (4% of eligible sales) and the sunset date. No broker note on the last call mentioned any of these.
2. **"Security-guard depth" for a manufacturer is the materials line, not the wage line.** Contract minimum-wage labour is ~0.3% of sales here (3–4 bps per 10% wage step) against VMM's 3.8%. The protocol's L4 default (wages, guards, rent) must be chosen by cost weight, not by habit.
3. **BRSR intensity ratios give physical volume for free.** Energy (GJ) ÷ GJ per unit gives "equivalent units" (~147.9k), cross-footed by water and waste. That splits growth into volume (+7%) and price/mix (+10%) with no company KPI needed.
4. **Find out who carries the timing mismatch.** Cost-plus purchases from sister companies plus fixed-price order books mean the listed minority absorbs commodity lags. That is a structural fact behind a "cyclical" margin dip.
5. **Physics checks work on demand claims too.** IT MW × PUE × redundancy × ₹/MW puts bounds on the whole DC genset market, and Cummins' DC revenue sits at its top. The gap is a research question, not a conclusion.
6. Time spent: about 75% on primary filings (AR notes, BRSR, AGM notice, 7 transcripts, postal ballot), 15% on estimates, 10% on web/peer. Broker notes were not needed. Analyst questions in transcripts relay what the sell side knows.
